title: U.S. House · Maryland's 6th District
area: Western Maryland and part of Montgomery County, including Hagerstown, Frederick and Gaithersburg.

context.text: Incumbent April McClain Delaney defeated David Trone and other Democratic primary candidates on June 23, 2026. Robin Ficker, a longtime Maryland political figure and repeat candidate, defeated Christopher Burnett and Mariela Roca in the Republican primary; former Rep. Neil Parrott did not make the ballot. Moshe Landman advanced on the Green Party line.

summary.text: April McClain Delaney is the Democratic incumbent in Maryland's 6th Congressional District, elected in 2024 to succeed David Trone. A communications lawyer, she worked for a children-and-technology nonprofit and, from 2022, at the U.S. Department of Commerce under President Biden before her election. She is running for a second term.

background.text: Born in Buhl, Idaho, in 1964. According to her congressional website, she grew up there as the daughter of a potato farmer.
Earned a bachelor's degree in communications from Northwestern University in 1986 and a law degree from Georgetown Law Center in 1989.
Began her career in communications law with the satellite firm Orion Network Systems, later becoming Washington director for Common Sense Media, a nonprofit focused on children and technology.

Joined the U.S. Department of Commerce in 2022 as deputy assistant secretary for communications and information at the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA). According to her website, her work there included broadband access and digital equity efforts and the First Responder Network.
Served on the boards of the Georgetown University Law Center, the International Center for Research on Women, and the Northwestern University School of Communications.
Won the 2024 general election for Maryland's 6th District with 53.0% of the vote over Republican Neil Parrott, and took office January 3, 2025 as the successor to David Trone.

Serves on the House Committee on Agriculture (subcommittees on Commodity Markets, Digital Assets, and Rural Development, and on Conservation, Research, and Biotechnology) and the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology (Research and Technology subcommittee).
Advanced from the June 23, 2026 Democratic primary. According to her website, she lives in Montgomery County with her husband, former Rep. John Delaney, and their four children.

priorities.text: Increasing economic opportunity and job growth by building partnerships that bring good-paying jobs to the district.
Leveraging technology to drive economic development across the 6th District.

positions.summary: Describes herself as an unwavering supporter of reproductive rights and the right to an abortion.
Joined the Maryland delegation in a letter urging House Republican leaders to extend the ACA enhanced premium tax credits and warning of Medicaid losses under H.R. 1.
positions.quote: we urge leadership to act swiftly to extend the ePTCs

positions.summary: Urged Congress to revoke President Trump's tariff authority, saying the tariffs raise costs for families, while also calling for a bipartisan strategy that combines carefully considered tariffs with incentives to rebuild American industry.
positions.quote: it is time for Congress to reclaim the authority to levy tariffs, as intended by the Constitution

positions.summary: Voted no on a February 2026 funding bill and said she opposes further DHS funding without guardrails such as a ban on ICE agents wearing masks, body cameras and an end to arrests without judicial warrants.
positions.quote: I remain opposed to any funding - for any length of time, even 10 days as laid out by this bill - to further fund the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) while it continues to terrorize American communities through unlawful raids, arrests, detentions, and discriminatory practices.

record.text: Serves on the House Committee on Agriculture and House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology for the 2025-2026 term.

summary.text: Robin Ficker is the Republican nominee for Maryland's 6th Congressional District. A former one-term member of the Maryland House of Delegates and longtime attorney and ballot-initiative activist, he has run for many offices since leaving the legislature. He was disbarred in 2022, and he won the June 23, 2026 Republican primary for this seat.

background.text: Born in Takoma Park, Maryland; attended Takoma Park Elementary and graduated from Montgomery Blair High School.

Earned a law degree from the University of Baltimore School of Law and a graduate degree from American University. Ballotpedia lists a West Point bachelor's degree while Wikipedia reports he attended the academy for five semesters and earned a B.S. from Case Western Reserve University, so the undergraduate degree is not stated here.

Practiced law as a member of the Maryland Bar from 1973 until he was disbarred in 2022; The Daily Record reports he later lost a bid to be reinstated. He has also been listed as a real estate broker and farmer.
Served one term in the Maryland House of Delegates (District 15B), 1979 to 1983.

Since the 1970s has promoted ballot initiatives in Montgomery County and Maryland. In his own words he has placed 25 ballot measures, including term limits for county officials and property tax revenue limits; a 2016 initiative he promoted imposed term limits on Montgomery County Council members.

Has run for office many times since 1978 without winning a general election, including a 2006 independent bid for Montgomery County Executive (28,063 votes), the 2012 Republican primary for this House seat, the 2018 Republican nomination for county executive, the 2022 Republican primary for governor, and the 2024 Republican primary for U.S. Senate (27.8%, second to Larry Hogan).
The Daily Record identifies him as 83 years old and from Boyds in Montgomery County.

priorities.text: Limiting property taxes and government spending.
Supporting small business and job growth.

record.text: As a private citizen, successfully placed a 2008 Montgomery County ballot measure requiring a unanimous County Council vote to raise property tax revenue faster than the rate of inflation.

candidates.name: Moshe Landman

summary.text: Moshe Landman is the Green Party nominee for Maryland's 6th Congressional District. An attorney and business founder with a background in real estate finance and artificial intelligence consulting, he previously ran for the Maryland State Senate in 2022. He describes his priorities as environmental repair, caring for people in need, and fiscal reform.

background.text: Born in Washington, D.C.; according to his Ballotpedia survey he grew up in Wheaton, Maryland, and is the son of a Silver Spring rabbi.

Earned a high school diploma from the Hebrew Academy of Greater Washington, a bachelor's degree from Yeshiva University (2000), a graduate degree from George Mason University (2003; described in his survey as an M.B.A.), and a J.D. from Georgetown University Law Center (2006).

Works as an attorney (he describes himself as licensed in New York), commercial mortgage broker, and artificial intelligence consultant, and founded Landman Law, Maryland Metal (a precious metal dealer), and Maryland Medicinals (a wellness company).
Says he was appointed as a voting member of the Montgomery County Forest Conservation Advisory Committee.
Ran as the Green Party candidate for Maryland State Senate District 39 in 2022, losing to Sen. Nancy King, 12.3% to 86.2%. He did not receive the Green Party nomination for this House seat in 2024.

priorities.text: Achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions and preserving natural resources, including implementing regenerative agriculture and a Green New Deal.
Implementing a universal health care system.
Significantly cutting military spending and creating what he calls a fair tax system.

positions.summary: Wants to commit to net-zero greenhouse gas emissions, clean up polluted mines and brownfields, and preserve 30% of lands and oceans.
Advocates implementing a universal health care system, which he says would save over 100,000 lives and $500 billion annually.
Campaign website calls for safe storage laws, more local authority to regulate firearms and microstamping requirements.
positions.quote: We should enact safe storage laws, increase local authority to regulate firearms, and create microstamping requirements.

positions.summary: Campaign website says corporations and the very wealthy should pay more in taxes so most people can pay less.
positions.quote: We can afford to cut taxes for most people if we make corporations and the super-rich pay their fair share.

positions.summary: Campaign website calls for a federally funded childcare program for pre-school and young school children.
positions.quote: A universal, federally funded childcare program for pre-school and young school children should be developed.

statements.quote: Immigration raids are terrorizing the immigrant community. Families are being broken up.
statements.context: On his campaign website Issues page, which states the campaign follows the Green Party platform (page undated; accessed Oct. 19, 2026)

candidates.researchNotes: Climate and health-care positions come from his 2025 Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey; additional positions and statements come from the Issues page of his campaign website, which presents Green Party platform language.

researchNotes: Biography gaps: Moshe Landman has no campaign website or news coverage found, so his biography rests on Ballotpedia and his own survey answers; Robin Ficker has no official biography, and sources disagree on his undergraduate degree.
